question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Ace in the hole
option_1: To create noisy disturbances so that competitors are unable to work.
option_2: A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time.
option_3: To attempt to do the impossible.
option_4: To suffer an injury on the lower body.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A major advantage that one keeps hidden until an ideal time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Ace in the hole" means a hidden advantage or resource kept in reserve until it is needed, especially to turn a situation in one's favour, and not revealed until the right moment. (गुप्त लाभ/तुरुप का पत्ता)
◦ Example: The lawyer kept the surprise witness as his ace in the hole for the final day of the trial.

• The expression comes from card games such as stud poker, where an "ace in the hole" is a face-down ace known only to its holder, giving them a hidden edge over the other players.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To create noisy disturbances so that competitors are unable to work is incorrect — this describes sabotage or disruption, which has no connection to a hidden reserve advantage.

• Option 3: To attempt to do the impossible is incorrect — this meaning is closer to idioms like "to reach for the moon", not "ace in the hole".

• Option 4: To suffer an injury on the lower body is incorrect — this is a purely literal, unrelated meaning with no idiomatic basis in the phrase.

NOTE

• Other idioms of hidden strength/advantage often asked in SSC: "Trump card" (a decisive resource kept for the right moment), "Up one's sleeve" (a secret plan or resource) and "In reserve" (kept back for future use).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Calibrate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gauge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Calibrate means to check, adjust, or determine (by comparison with a standard) the graduations of a measuring instrument, or more generally to measure something precisely. (सही मापना/अंशांकन करना)
◦ Example: The technician had to calibrate the thermometer before using it in the lab.

• Gauge (as a verb) means to measure exactly, or to estimate/judge the amount, level or dimension of something, which is the closest match in meaning to "calibrate" among the given options. (मापना/आकलन करना)
◦ Example: It is difficult to gauge how the public will react to the new policy.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Gauze is incorrect — it means a thin, light, transparent fabric, often used for bandages or curtains; it is a homophone-like word confused with "Gauge" but has an entirely different meaning.

• Option 2: Assail is incorrect — it means to attack someone or something violently, physically or verbally.

• Option 4: Affront is incorrect — it means an action or remark that insults or offends someone.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the spellings "Gauge" (to measure) and "Gauze" (a thin fabric) — they are frequently used as distractors in SSC vocabulary questions.

• Related words: calibration (noun), calibrated (adjective), calibrator (an instrument used to calibrate).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
The social ______ is going to meet with all of us tomorrow with the plans so we can make a decision.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. worker.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "social worker" is a person whose job is to help individuals, families and communities with their problems, often on behalf of a government or welfare organisation, and who typically attends meetings to discuss plans and decisions — which fits the context of the sentence perfectly. (समाज सेवक)
◦ Example: The social worker met with all of us tomorrow with the plans so we can make a decision.

• The sentence requires a noun that collocates with "social" and can plausibly attend a meeting to discuss plans — "social worker" is the standard fixed collocation used in such contexts.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: army is incorrect — "social army" is not a meaningful or standard collocation in English.

• Option 3: toddler is incorrect — a toddler is a very young child; it makes no logical sense for a toddler to hold a meeting about plans and decisions.

• Option 4: labour is incorrect — "social labour" is not the natural collocation here; "labour" refers to work/workforce in general, not a person who can attend a meeting.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with "social": social worker, social media, social gathering, social security, social distancing.

• Such contextual fill-in-the-blank questions are best solved by identifying the natural collocation that fits both the grammar and the real-world logic of the sentence.

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
He has been / told many a times to / mind his manners.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. told many a times to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "many a times". The correct form is "many a time" (singular), not "many a times" (plural).

• Rule — "Many a + singular noun": The structure "many a" is always followed by a singular countable noun and takes a singular verb, even though the meaning is plural. This is a fixed, idiomatic construction.
◦ Example: Many a soldier has died for his country. (NOT: many a soldiers/many a times)

• Applying the rule, "many a times" must be corrected to "many a time", giving: He has been told many a time to mind his manners.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: No error is incorrect because there clearly is a grammatical error in the sentence, as explained above.

• Option 2: He has been is incorrect because this part is grammatically correct — it is simply the present perfect passive auxiliary "has been", used correctly here.

• Option 4: mind his manners. is incorrect because this part is a correct, idiomatic phrase meaning "to behave politely"; it contains no grammatical error.

NOTE

• Other constructions similar to "many a": "many a time", "many a man", "many a book" — always singular noun + singular verb.

• Contrast this with "a number of", which takes a plural noun and plural verb, e.g. "A number of students were present."

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
In humans, lack of sleep leads to ______ memory and reduced cognitive abilities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. impaired.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Impaired means weakened, damaged, or made less effective in function, which fits the context of memory being negatively affected by lack of sleep. (क्षीण/कमजोर)
◦ Example: Lack of sleep leads to impaired memory and reduced cognitive abilities.

• The sentence discusses a negative consequence of sleep deprivation on both memory and cognitive abilities, so the missing word must carry a negative sense parallel to "reduced" — "impaired" fits this logic exactly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: attended is incorrect — it means "looked after" or "was present at"; it does not fit the negative sense required by the sentence.

• Option 3: thankless is incorrect — it means "not likely to be appreciated"; it describes a task or effort, not a mental faculty like memory.

• Option 4: witnessed is incorrect — it means "saw something happen"; "witnessed memory" is not a meaningful collocation.

NOTE

• Words related in meaning to "impaired": weakened, diminished, deteriorated, compromised.

• Common collocations: impaired vision, impaired judgment, impaired hearing, impaired memory.

question:
The given sentence is in active voice. Change the voice of the sentence. Select the correct option from the sentences given in options.
The story explores the conflicting range of human emotions.
option_1: The conflicting range of human emotions had explored by the story.
option_2: The conflicting range of human emotions did explored by the story.
option_3: The conflicting range of human emotions is explored by the story.
option_4: The conflicting range of human emotions has explored by the story.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The conflicting range of human emotions is explored by the story.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The story explores the conflicting range of human emotions" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the conflicting range of human emotions" becomes the subject; being singular, it takes the auxiliary "is"; the verb "explores" becomes the past participle "explored"; and "the story" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The conflicting range of human emotions is explored by the story.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "had explored" is a past participle form used with Past Perfect Tense passives ("had been explored"), and is grammatically malformed here without "been".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "did explored" is ungrammatical — "did" (a Simple Past auxiliary) must be followed by the base form, not the past participle, and in any case this is not a valid passive structure.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has explored" is missing the required "been" for a Present Perfect passive ("has been explored"), and does not match the Simple Present tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Common passive-voice traps in SSC: auxiliary verbs (is/am/are/was/were/has been/had been) must match both the tense of the original sentence and the number (singular/plural) of the new subject.

• Always convert the main verb to its third form (V3) in passive voice, never leave it in base or past-tense form.

question:
Some parts of one or more sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
At Paris, just after dark
A. of meditation and a meerschaum, in company
B. one gusty evening in the autumn
C. of 18, I was enjoying the twofold luxury
D. with my friend Auguste Dupin, in his little back library
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BCAD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening phrase "At Paris, just after dark" must be followed logically by a time expression, then the description of the activity, and finally the companion and location — this chain of logic decides the correct sequence.

• Sequencing logic: B ("one gusty evening in the autumn") specifies exactly when, continuing directly from "just after dark"; C ("of 18--, I was enjoying the twofold luxury") completes the year reference from B and introduces the main clause "I was enjoying..."; A ("of meditation and a meerschaum, in company") completes "the twofold luxury of" from C and begins the companionship clause; D ("with my friend Auguste Dupin, in his little back library") completes "in company with" from A and closes the sentence with the location.

• Reconstructed sentence: "At Paris, just after dark, one gusty evening in the autumn of 18--, I was enjoying the twofold luxury of meditation and a meerschaum, in company with my friend Auguste Dupin, in his little back library."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (BCAD).

Additional Information

• Option 1: CDBA is incorrect because it places "of 18, I was enjoying..." immediately after the opening phrase, before the time reference "one gusty evening" is established, breaking the logical flow.

• Option 2: ADBC is incorrect because it introduces "of meditation and a meerschaum" before the clause "I was enjoying the twofold luxury" that it is meant to complete, making the sentence meaningless.

• Option 4: DCBA is incorrect because it starts with the companionship clause "with my friend Auguste Dupin" before any main clause or time reference has been introduced, producing a grammatically broken sentence.

NOTE

• In parajumble/sentence-rearrangement questions, look first for a part that grammatically completes a phrase begun in the fixed sentence or another labelled part — this quickly narrows down the starting and ending parts.

• Pronoun and possessive references (e.g. "my friend") and connecting words (e.g. "of", "with", "in company") are the strongest clues to sequence such jumbled parts correctly.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
I just don't like the themes of todays music.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. todays music.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word "todays". It is a possessive noun modifying "music" (the music belonging to/of today) and therefore must carry an apostrophe before the "s": "today's".

• Rule — Possessive apostrophe: A singular noun forms its possessive by adding apostrophe + s ('s). Without the apostrophe, "todays" is not a grammatically valid word in this possessive sense.
◦ Example: today's music, today's newspaper, today's youth.

• Applying the rule, the corrected sentence reads: "I just don't like the themes of today's music."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: No error is incorrect because there clearly is a punctuation/grammar error in the sentence, as explained above.

• Option 2: I just don't is incorrect because this part is correctly written, with the contraction "don't" correctly punctuated with an apostrophe.

• Option 3: like the themes of is incorrect because this part contains no grammatical or spelling error; it is a straightforward correct phrase.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the possessive apostrophe (today's = of today) with a plural form (todays would wrongly suggest more than one "today", which is not standard usage).

• Similar commonly tested possessive forms: yesterday's news, tomorrow's meeting, the world's population, India's economy.

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given group of words.
A man who is womanish in his habits
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Effeminate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Effeminate means a man who has qualities, habits, or manners more traditionally associated with women; womanish in habits or appearance. (स्त्रैण/जनखा स्वभाव वाला)
◦ Example: His effeminate mannerisms often drew comments from his classmates.

• One-word substitutions like this are tested by matching the exact defining phrase given in the question to the single word that captures its full meaning — here "womanish in his habits" maps precisely onto "effeminate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Indictment is incorrect — it means a formal charge or accusation of a serious crime. (अभियोग)

• Option 3: Hooch is incorrect — it is an informal word for illegally made alcoholic liquor. (अवैध शराब)

• Option 4: Infidel is incorrect — it means a person who does not believe in a particular religion, especially one considered the main religion by a group. (नास्तिक/काफ़िर)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often confused in SSC: Misogynist (a man who hates women), Misanthrope (one who hates mankind in general), Philanderer (a man who has many casual affairs with women).

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. more stringent mobility control and physical distancing policies
Q. East Asian governments (except for Japan) implemented
R. as well as more comprehensive testing, tracing
S. and isolation policies since the early stages
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. QPRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must begin with the grammatical subject and verb before any object can follow, so Q ("East Asian governments (except for Japan) implemented") must come first, as it is the only part with a clear subject and main verb.

• Sequencing logic: Q introduces "implemented", which needs an object — P ("more stringent mobility control and physical distancing policies") supplies that object; R ("as well as more comprehensive testing, tracing") adds a second list of measures using the connector "as well as"; S ("and isolation policies since the early stages") completes the list begun in R ("testing, tracing and isolation policies") and adds the time reference.

• Reconstructed sentence: "East Asian governments (except for Japan) implemented more stringent mobility control and physical distancing policies as well as more comprehensive testing, tracing and isolation policies since the early stages."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (QPRS).

Additional Information

• Option 1: PSRQ is incorrect because it begins with the object "more stringent mobility control..." before any subject or verb has been introduced, making the sequence ungrammatical.

• Option 3: PRSQ is incorrect for the same reason — it starts with the object part P instead of the subject-verb part Q.

• Option 4: QSPR is incorrect because after "implemented" (Q), it jumps to S ("and isolation policies...") which cannot logically or grammatically follow "implemented" without its object P coming first.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement (parajumble) questions, always look first for the part containing the main subject and finite verb — that part almost always opens the sentence.

• Connecting words such as "as well as", "and", "since" are strong clues for linking the remaining parts in the correct logical order.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Over and above
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. In addition to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom/phrase "Over and above" means besides, in addition to, or as well as something already mentioned. (के अतिरिक्त/के अलावा)
◦ Example: Over and above his salary, he receives a generous travel allowance.

• The phrase is used to introduce something extra that is added to what has already been stated, which is exactly what "in addition to" conveys.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Above all is incorrect — it means "most importantly of all", used to emphasise the most significant point, not to add something extra.

• Option 2: To sum up the conversation is incorrect — this describes concluding or summarising, which is unrelated to "over and above".

• Option 4: Highest rank is incorrect — this is a literal, unrelated meaning; "over and above" is not used to indicate rank or hierarchy.

NOTE

• Other idioms of addition often asked in SSC: "In addition to", "On top of", "Not to mention", "Along with" — all used to introduce something extra beyond what is already stated.

• Do not confuse "Over and above" (in addition to) with "Above all" (most importantly) — both contain "above" but carry different meanings.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
In this engineering design project you will learn how to build an infinity mirror, with built-in lights that make the mirror look like a deep ______ with no end.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. tunnel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "tunnel" is a long, narrow underground or enclosed passage, and the phrase "a deep tunnel with no end" vividly describes the illusion of infinite depth created by an infinity mirror. (सुरंग)
◦ Example: The built-in lights make the mirror look like a deep tunnel with no end.

• The sentence describes a visual illusion of endless depth, which logically and idiomatically matches the image of a "tunnel", a common way to describe infinity-mirror effects.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: lodge is incorrect — a lodge is a small house or cabin; it does not fit the description of endless visual depth.

• Option 3: funeral is incorrect — a funeral is a ceremony for the dead; it has no connection to a mirror's visual illusion of depth.

• Option 4: signal is incorrect — a signal is a sign or gesture conveying information; "a deep signal with no end" is not meaningful.

NOTE

• Contextual fill-in-the-blank questions like this are best solved by visualising the scene described and picking the noun that most naturally completes the image.

• Words associated with depth/infinity imagery: abyss, chasm, void, tunnel, corridor.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Book giving information about everything
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Encyclopedia.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Encyclopedia" is a book or set of books giving information on many subjects or on many aspects of one subject, typically arranged alphabetically. (विश्वकोश)
◦ Example: She looked up the topic of ancient Rome in the encyclopedia.

• The defining phrase "book giving information about everything" precisely matches the comprehensive, all-subject nature of an encyclopedia.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Dictionary is incorrect — a dictionary gives the meanings, spellings and pronunciations of words, not general information about all subjects.

• Option 3: Phonebook is incorrect — a phonebook is a directory listing telephone numbers and addresses, not general knowledge.

• Option 4: Thesis is incorrect — a thesis is a long research essay or dissertation written on one specific topic, usually for a degree, not a general information book.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Glossary (a list of specialised terms with their meanings), Anthology (a collection of selected literary pieces), Bibliography (a list of books/sources referred to in a work).

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
WHIMSICAL
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. FUNNY.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Whimsical means playful, quaint, or unpredictable in a light-hearted, amusing way; given to fanciful or odd ideas. (सनकी/विचित्र किन्तु मनोरंजक)
◦ Example: The film had a whimsical charm that made audiences smile throughout.

• Among the given options, "FUNNY" is the closest in spirit to "whimsical", since both describe something amusing, light-hearted and pleasantly unusual, whereas the other options describe entirely unrelated qualities.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: WEAK is incorrect — it means lacking strength or power, which is unrelated to playful unpredictability.

• Option 2: RESPECTFUL is incorrect — it means showing deference or esteem for someone, which has no connection to whimsy.

• Option 3: HUMILIATED is incorrect — it means made to feel ashamed or foolish, the opposite mood of light-hearted whimsy.

NOTE

• Words close in meaning to "whimsical": fanciful, quirky, capricious, playful, eccentric.

• Do not confuse "whimsical" (playful/fanciful) with "capricious" in its negative sense of being unpredictably changeable in mood or behaviour — in SSC vocabulary lists the two are often paired as near-synonyms.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Instigate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Raise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Instigate means to bring about or initiate an action, especially by encouraging or provoking others; to stir up or incite. (भड़काना/उकसाना)
◦ Example: The rumour instigated a wave of panic among the villagers.

• Raise here is used in the sense of "to bring about, stir up, or set in motion" (as in "to raise a rebellion" or "to raise trouble"), which is the closest match to "instigate" among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Deterrence is incorrect — it means the act of discouraging or preventing an action, which is nearly opposite in sense to "instigate".

• Option 2: Settle is incorrect — it means to resolve a dispute or come to rest, which is unrelated to provoking or inciting.

• Option 4: Complaisance is incorrect — it means a willingness to please others or comply agreeably, which has no connection to inciting action.

NOTE

• Words close in meaning to "instigate": incite, provoke, foment, stir up, spur, kindle.

• Its near-opposite words: deter, discourage, restrain, suppress.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Inept
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Competent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Inept means having or showing no skill; clumsy or incompetent in performing a task. (अयोग्य/अनाड़ी)

• Competent means having the necessary ability, skill, or knowledge to do something successfully, which is the direct opposite of "inept". (योग्य/सक्षम)
◦ Example: Despite being new to the job, she proved to be a competent manager, quite unlike her inept predecessor.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Wanting is incorrect — it means lacking or deficient in something, which is actually close in sense to "inept" rather than opposite to it.

• Option 3: Barred is incorrect — it means prohibited or excluded, which is unrelated to skill or competence.

• Option 4: Callow is incorrect — it means inexperienced or immature, which is closer in sense to "inept" (lacking skill due to inexperience) rather than its opposite.

NOTE

• Words close in meaning to "inept": clumsy, incompetent, unskilful, bungling.

• Other antonym pairs commonly tested: adept/inept, proficient/incompetent, skilful/clumsy.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Frighter.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Freighter" — a large ship or aircraft that carries goods, or a person/company that arranges the transport of goods. "Frighter" is an incorrect spelling.

• Spelling key: FREIGHT + ER. Note the "ei" in "freight" (as in the noun "freight" meaning goods transported in bulk), which is missing in the wrongly spelt "Frighter".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Practical" is correctly spelt — meaning relating to practice or action rather than theory.

• Option 2: "Glowing" is correctly spelt — the present participle of "glow", meaning shining with a warm, steady light, or highly favourable (as in "glowing praise").

• Option 3: "Released" is correctly spelt — the past tense of "release", meaning to set free or make available.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Freighter" (a cargo ship/aircraft) with "Frighten" (to scare) — the two share no spelling relationship, and "Frighter" is not a valid word in English.

• Other words with the tricky "eigh" pattern: weight, height, neighbour, eight, freight.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: The joy definitely lies in cooking for others.
option_2: The joy definitely lyes in cooking for others.
option_3: The joy defintely lies in cooking for others.
option_4: The joy definitely lies in cokking for others.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The joy definitely lies in cooking for others.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 1 contains all correctly spelt words: "definitely" (not "defintely"), "lies" (not "lyes"), and "cooking" (not "cokking").

• Spelling key: "definitely" = DE + FIN + ITE + LY (commonly misspelt as "defintely" by dropping the first "i"); "lies" is the correct present-tense form of "to lie" (not "lyes", which is not an English word); "cooking" is spelt with a double "o" (not "cokking", with a double "k").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "lyes" is a misspelling of "lies".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "defintely" is a misspelling of "definitely" (the "i" after "def" is missing).

• Option 4 is incorrect because "cokking" is a misspelling of "cooking" (it wrongly doubles the "k" instead of the "o").

NOTE

• "Definitely" is one of the most commonly misspelt words in English — remember it contains "finite" within it: defINITEly.

• Always double-check silent/doubled letters in common verbs like "cooking", "running", "stopping" — the doubling rule depends on the base word's final consonant and preceding vowel.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A lover of oneself, of one's advancement
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Egoist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Egoist" is a person who is excessively concerned with themselves and their own advancement, interests, or well-being; a self-centred person. (स्वार्थी/अहंवादी)
◦ Example: He was such an egoist that he never considered how his decisions affected others.

• The defining phrase "a lover of oneself, of one's advancement" describes exactly this self-centred, self-promoting quality captured by "egoist".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Philistine is incorrect — it means a person who is hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts. (कलाविरोधी/असंस्कृत व्यक्ति)

• Option 2: Mercenary is incorrect — it means a person primarily motivated by monetary gain, especially a soldier who fights for whoever pays them. (भाड़े का सैनिक/स्वार्थलोलुप)

• Option 3: Cynic is incorrect — it means a person who believes that people are motivated only by self-interest and distrusts sincerity in others. (निंदक/संशयवादी)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often confused with "Egoist": Narcissist (a person with an excessive admiration of their own appearance/abilities), Altruist (the opposite — one who selflessly cares for others' welfare).

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
Gloria said, “His relatives are landing tomorrow.”
option_1: Gloria said that his relatives are landing the next day.
option_2: Gloria said that his relatives were landing the previous day.
option_3: Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.
option_4: Gloria said that his relatives have been landing the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reporting verb "said" is in the past tense (with no reporting object), so the tense of the reported speech must be backshifted by one degree, and time/place expressions must also change accordingly.

• Rule — Direct to Indirect (Present Continuous):
◦ Direct: Subject + say(s)/said + "Subject + is/am/are + V-ing..."
◦ Indirect: Subject + said + that + Subject + was/were + V-ing...

• Applying the rule: "are landing" (Present Continuous) changes to "were landing" (Past Continuous), and the time word "tomorrow" changes to "the next day".
◦ Indirect: Gloria said that his relatives were landing the next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "are landing" has not been backshifted to the past tense as required when the reporting verb "said" is in the past.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "the previous day" is the wrong time-shift for "tomorrow" — "tomorrow" correctly changes to "the next day", not "the previous day" (which is the change for "yesterday").

• Option 4 is incorrect because "have been landing" (Present Perfect Continuous) is the wrong backshifted tense; Present Continuous correctly backshifts to Past Continuous ("were landing"), not Present Perfect Continuous.

NOTE

• Common time-word changes in narration: today → that day; tomorrow → the next day/the following day; yesterday → the previous day/the day before; now → then; here → there.

• Tense backshift chart: Present Simple → Past Simple; Present Continuous → Past Continuous; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; Simple Past → Past Perfect.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.

Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

People may seek fashion as part of (1) ______ they are and may want to be a fashion lover, which may lead them to spend more time (2) ______ out the latest fashion trends and more money than others on fashion products. We all know the good feeling that goes (3) ______ walking out of a store with a new shade of lipstick or after ordering a killer pair of boots online. They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. who.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrase "as part of who they are", an idiomatic expression meaning "as part of their identity/character". The relative/interrogative pronoun "who" is used here to refer to a person's identity as a person (subject reference), which is the standard idiom.

• Rule: "Who" is used to refer to a person acting as the subject of the clause it introduces (here, functioning within the fixed expression "part of who they are", referring to their identity), whereas "whom" refers to the object, "whose" shows possession, and "which" refers to things, not people.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: which is incorrect — "which" is used for things or animals, not for a person's identity in this idiomatic expression.

• Option 2: whom is incorrect — "whom" is the objective case, used when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition within its own clause, which does not fit here.

• Option 3: whose is incorrect — "whose" indicates possession ("belonging to whom"), which does not fit the sense of "part of who they are" (their identity).

NOTE

• Fixed idiomatic phrase: "part of who [someone] is/are" — meaning an inherent part of a person's identity or character.

• Quick rule for who/whom/whose/which: who (subject, people), whom (object, people), whose (possession), which/that (things).

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. seeking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrasal verb "seeking out", which means to search for and find something, especially something desired, here referring to actively searching for the latest fashion trends.

• Rule — Phrasal verb collocation: The phrase "spend time seeking out [something]" is a standard, idiomatic collocation meaning to actively look for and follow something of interest.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: freaking is incorrect — "freaking out" means to become extremely upset or excited, which does not fit the neutral context of following fashion trends.

• Option 3: doing is incorrect — "doing out the latest fashion trends" is not a valid or meaningful phrasal verb combination.

• Option 4: making is incorrect — "making out" means to discern or manage, or informally to kiss; it does not collocate meaningfully with "the latest fashion trends" here.

NOTE

• Other common "seek" phrasal expressions: seek out (search for), seek after (pursue), seek to (attempt to).

• Cloze passages often test correct phrasal-verb collocations — always check which verb naturally pairs with the preposition/particle already given in the sentence.

question:

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. along with.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrase "the good feeling that goes along with walking out of a store...", where "goes along with" means accompanies or is associated with.

• Rule — Phrasal collocation: "Goes along with" is a fixed expression meaning that one thing naturally accompanies or is a consequence of another; it correctly links the "good feeling" to the act of shopping described afterward.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: off in is incorrect — "goes off in" is not a standard or meaningful collocation in this context.

• Option 2: within is incorrect — "goes within" does not form a meaningful phrase with "the good feeling"; "within" typically indicates something inside a boundary, not an accompanying feeling.

• Option 3: up in is incorrect — "goes up in" typically relates to something increasing or going up in flames/smoke, which does not fit here.

NOTE

• Common phrasal expressions with "go": go along with (accompany/agree with), go through with (complete despite difficulty), go without (manage without something), go over (review).

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. backed up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrase "more than one scientific study has backed up its effectiveness", where "backed up" means supported or confirmed with evidence.

• Rule — Phrasal verb meaning: "Back up" means to support a claim, statement, or theory with evidence or proof, which fits the context of scientific studies confirming the effectiveness of "retail therapy".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: held back is incorrect — "held back" means restrained or prevented from advancing, which contradicts the positive sense of confirming effectiveness.

• Option 2: summed up is incorrect — "summed up" means summarised briefly; a study does not "sum up" effectiveness, it supports or confirms it.

• Option 4: sold on is incorrect — "sold on" means convinced or enthusiastic about something; while related in tone, a "study" is not naturally said to be "sold on" its own effectiveness — it "backs up" or supports the claim with evidence.

NOTE

• Common phrasal expressions with "back": back up (support with evidence), back down (withdraw from a position), back out (withdraw from a commitment).

• In cloze passages, always match the phrasal verb's idiomatic meaning to the logical relationship being described (here, evidence confirming a claim).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.

Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

People may seek fashion as part of (1) ______ they are and may want to be a fashion lover, which may lead them to spend more time (2) ______ out the latest fashion trends and more money than others on fashion products. We all know the good feeling that goes (3) ______ walking out of a store with a new shade of lipstick or after ordering a killer pair of boots online. They call it retail therapy for a reason, and more than one scientific study has (4) ______ its effectiveness. Shopping takes time and concentration, whether it is being done online (5) ______ in your favourite store.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. or.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the correlative structure "whether it is being done online or in your favourite store", presenting two alternative possibilities.

• Rule — Correlative conjunction "whether...or": The conjunction "whether" is always paired with "or" to present two (or more) alternatives, and this is a fixed grammatical pairing in English.
◦ Example: I don't know whether he will come or stay back.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: if is incorrect — "whether...if" is not a valid correlative pairing; "if" is not used to complete the "whether" structure.

• Option 2: and is incorrect — "and" would suggest both options happen together (online and in-store), not that they are alternatives, which contradicts the intended sense of "whether".

• Option 4: so is incorrect — "so" indicates a result or consequence, not an alternative, and does not grammatically pair with "whether".

NOTE

• Fixed correlative conjunction pairs frequently tested in SSC: whether...or, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and.

• Never mix these pairs (e.g. "either...nor" or "neither...or" are incorrect combinations).
